newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NEW BBL CHIEF SEES "STAND-ALONE" FUTURE FOR BANK.
newsitem.headline: NEW BBL CHIEF SEES "STAND-ALONE" FUTURE FOR BANK.

text.p: Michel Tilmant, chief executive officer of Banque Bruxelles Lambert (BBL) since January 1, said on Wednesday he saw the future of his bank in a "stand alone" perspective.
His predecessor, Daniel Cardon, had repeatedly said he considered BBL was too small and that he wanted a partner for the bank to face the challenges of the European single currency.
"We are happy bachelors, but we are attentive. If we marry, it must be so that we are happier after than before," he said.
He said that any alliance or merger would have to respect the needs and rights of customers, personnel, shareholders and the broader society.

"Our bank is capable of building its future alone. But if any opportunities arise, we will definitely look at them. If either management or the shareholders make a proposal, it will be studied," he said.
Asked about a proposal last year by Belgian holding company Societe Generale de Belgique SA (SGB) to merge SGB unit Generale Bank with BBL, Tilmant said:
"I was in favour of this project. But for reasons we all know this could not proceed. It is therefore now in the fridge...there are no plans to take this idea out of the fridge right now."
SGB chief executive Etienne Davignon said last year that a Generale Bank-BBL merger had been blocked by BBL minority shareholder Internationale Nederlanden Groep (ING).

Asked whether a merger with Generale Bank would not by definition cost jobs and lead to branch closures -- both banks are very similar in geographical coverage and product range -- Tilmant said: "A merger could have advantages for the domestic network, we would increase our marketing power."
Generale Bank is Belgium's biggest bank, BBL is number three.

Paribas Bank Belgium chief executive officer Philippe Romagnoli said last month that at least three top Belgian banks should merge to create a player that is fit to tackle the larger market created by the single currency.
Tilmant's predecessor Cardon had also repeatedly said that he considered BBL was too small.
"There is no critical mass or optimal size. If you want to be a big universal bank, size is important. If you want to be a small asset manager, then it is not," he said.
Tilmant insisted that he was not at odds with his predecessor about BBL's future.
"The sole difference is that last year, there was a concrete project. This is now in the fridge," he said.
BBL shares have carried a takeover premium for several years, as the market considers that the bank's disparate shareholdership structure makes it ripe for a merger operation.
At the end of 1996, Belgian holding company Groupe Bruxelles Lambert SA (GBL), traditionaly the leading shareholder in BBL, had a stake of 12.44 percent.

GBL last year signed a three-way shareholder pact for the control of BBL with insurer Royale Belge SA, which holds 12.37 percent and with bank Credit Communal/ Gemeentekrediet, which owns 12.33 percent.
The pact is currently under European Union competion authorities' scrutiny.
Dutch ING owns a 13.40 percent stake and controls the voting rights over another 6.73 percent, while Swiss Winterthur owns 8.23 percent.
-- Geert De Clercq, Brussels Newsroom +32 2 287 6813, Fax +32 2 230 7710
